title: sequence-tail-merging-soft-pad-and-kernel-prober-playbook
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes an operational playbook for reducing per-token cost and improving throughput by opportunistically merging sequence tails and using a soft-padding policy together with an online kernel prober (regressor + confidence) to select the best kernel variant for each merged shape. The key idea is to exploit the heavy tail of short requests: instead of force-padding each request to a strict bucket boundary, allow small, bounded tail merges and let the kernel prober guide whether the merged shape should pick a performance-optimized kernel or a conservative fallback.

Motivation and problem statement:

- We observe a bimodal length distribution across many workloads: a large number of short requests (<= 64 tokens) and a smaller number of long requests. Strict bucketing and hard padding waste compute on short requests and increase average latency under load.
- Current bucketing policies either overpad (wasting GPU cycles) or fragment batches into many small groups (losing packing efficiency).
- Kernel variant performance is shape-dependent. A kernel optimized for long sequences may underperform on tiny merged shapes and vice versa.
- KV cache reuse complicates merging: if merged sequences have different prefixes, naive merging breaks cache locality and increases memory copies.

Goals:

1) Reduce average per-token GPU cycles for short-to-medium requests by 10–30% in typical web workloads.
2) Maintain 99th percentile latency within SLOs (e.g., 95 ms P99 for tier-1).
3) Avoid KV cache invalidation regressions: ensure hit rate drop <= 2% after rollout.
4) Provide safe rollback and observability during incremental deployment.

Design overview (high level):

A. Tail merging window: hold short requests for up to W ms (configurable per model/tier, default 8ms) to opportunistically merge tails into a single packed batch. Merge candidates are sequences that arrive within W and whose combined padded shape stays under a per-model padding budget (B%) relative to sum-of-lengths.

B. Soft-pad policy: instead of padding every sequence to the next bucket, compute a minimal merged matrix shape by compacting tails (e.g., pack 38+22 => a 64-width row rather than two 38 and 22 buckets) if padding overhead <= padding_threshold (default 12%). Soft-pad allows small cross-request padding to enable better packing.

C. Kernel prober (online regressor): an online lightweight regressor that recommends kernel variant for a given merged shape based on features: (total_tokens, max_seq_len, mean_seq_len, prefix-hash-stability, device-temp, batch-size, recent-queue-latency). The prober emits (kernel_id, confidence_score). High-confidence picks are used; low-confidence decisions fallback to a conservative kernel that is robust across shapes. Confidence decays over time; prober updates from telemetry and occasional randomized A/B trials.

D. KV cache invariants: do not coalesce requests that would break prefix-invariant caching semantics. We define three safe merge classes:
  - Prefix-equal merges: same prefix fingerprint => safe to merge and share KV warmup.
  - Disjoint-prefix merges with independent KV contexts: allowed if the runtime can maintain separate KV buffers per request within the same batch without extra copies (hardware permitting).
  - Mixed-prefix soft merges (allowed but restricted): only if combined KV warmup cost is lower than threshold and KV-copy overhead is accounted as padding budget.

Heuristics and concrete algorithms:

1) Admission: when a short request arrives, compute a candidate merge set among currently waiting short requests (by arrival time) that:
   - have compatible model version and dtype/quantization profile,
   - have prefix-fingerprint delta <= prefix_threshold OR our runtime can isolate KV contexts cheaply,
   - joining them will not push padding overhead above B% (configurable), and
   - expected P99 increase (estimated via lookup table) is <= SLO_headroom.

2) Packing: use a greedy-first-fit with limited lookahead (k=4) to minimize wasted columns. Prefer merges that keep max_seq_len small (reduce KV width).

3) Kernel selection flow:
   - Query prober with merged-shape features.
   - If prober.confidence >= conf_threshold (e.g., 0.75), pick prober.kernel_id.
   - Else, select fallback-kernel (conservative) and schedule an asynchronous micro-A/B probe for this shape (1% of such decisions) to update prober offline.

4) KV handling: maintain per-request meta with KV-offsets. When merging, create either shared KV viewport (for prefix-equal) or vector-of-views mapping each sequence to its KV slices. If memory pressure prevents vector-of-views, the admission step denies merge.

Telemetry and metrics to collect (minimum):

- Merge rate: % of short requests that were merged.
- Padding delta: additional tokens introduced by soft-pad policy vs baseline.
- Kernel pick distribution: (kernel_id -> count) and per-kernel latency breakdown.
- Prober accuracy/confidence calibration: fraction of high-confidence picks that beat fallback.
- KV hit rate and average KV warmup time.
- SLOs: P50/P95/P99 latency for merged vs unmerged flows; tail error rate.

Experimentation plan (offline + online):

1) Offline profiling: run microbenchmarks across shape-grid for each kernel variant to build initial prober training set (features -> latency/cost). Store as N (shape->performance) table.
2) Canary: enable merge+softpad in a single region model under a synthetic traffic replay reproducing real arrival patterns (traffic from production trace). Verify merge rate and padding delta.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% rollouts gated by: P99 latency within SLO, KV hit rate regressions within threshold, and cost-per-token improvement.

Safety knobs and rollback strategies:

- Immediate: per-model kill-switch that disables tail merging or forces kernel to conservative fallback.
- Rapid rollback: if P99 exceeds threshold or KV hit rate drops >2%, undo merge within 30s via control-plane flag.
- Circuit breaker: if prober selects a kernel that produces hardware exceptions or memory OOMs > N, automatically mark kernel as banned for that shape.

Operational notes and open questions:

- How to set per-model padding_budget B%? Suggest a default of 12% but calibrate by model family (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder). Some models benefit from looser budgets.
- Prefix fingerprinting cost and collision rate tradeoffs: choose fast non-cryptographic hash (xxhash64) with small collision risk; collisions should be monitored.
- How to account for KV memory fragmentation when using vector-of-views? Need an allocator plan to avoid OOMs in p99 cases.
- Interaction with current batching and autoscaler: merged batches may increase instantaneous utilization spikes; ensure autoscaler tolerates short bursts.

Work items (next steps):

- Implementation spike: prober stub + offline profiler (owner: Aisha, ETA 2w).
- Admission/packing prototype in packer module (owner: Daniel, ETA 3w).
- KV-view allocator improvements (owner: Priya, ETA 3w).
- Canary config + dashboards (owner: Elena, ETA 1w).

Appendix: small pseudocode for admission path:

  on_short_request(req):
    candidates = windowed_queue.peek(W)
    best_group = greedy_pack(candidates, req)
    if padding_overhead(best_group) <= B and prefix_ok(best_group):
      merged = create_merged_batch(best_group)
      kernel, conf = prober.pick(merged.features)
      if conf < conf_threshold:
        kernel = conservative_kernel
        schedule_probe(merged.features)
      schedule(merged, kernel)
    else:
      schedule_single(req)

References and related artifacts:

- Existing playbooks on tail compaction and prefix-aware routing (see linked artifacts).
- Prior kernel benchmarking sheets (internal perf repo).

This doc is intentionally pragmatic and playbook-oriented: the goal is to get a safe, observable rollout that measurably reduces unit compute while keeping latency and KV semantics intact. Feedback welcome on thresholds and KV policy alternatives.
